what_its_for: Imiquimod is a cream used to treat certain skin conditions including genital and anal warts, a type of pre-cancerous skin growth on the face or scalp called actinic keratosis, and a type of early skin cancer called superficial basal cell carcinoma. It works by helping your own immune system fight abnormal skin cells and certain viruses.
how_to_take: Wash your hands before and after applying this cream. Clean and dry the treatment area completely before use. Apply a thin layer of cream to the affected skin and rub it in gently until the cream disappears. Do not cover the treated area with bandages or tight clothing after applying. Leave the cream on the skin for the recommended number of hours, then wash it off thoroughly with mild soap and water. Avoid getting the cream in your eyes, mouth, nose, or vagina.
dosing: The dose depends on what you are treating. For genital and anal warts: Apply the cream 3 times per week (for example, Monday, Wednesday, Friday) at bedtime. Leave it on for 6 to 10 hours, then wash off. For actinic keratosis (Aldara): Apply the cream 2 times per week for 16 weeks at bedtime. Leave on for 8 hours, then wash off. For superficial basal cell carcinoma (Aldara): Apply the cream 5 times per week (Monday through Friday) at bedtime for 6 weeks. Leave on for 8 hours, then wash off. Always follow the exact instructions given by your doctor or pharmacist, as your dose may be different.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, apply it as soon as you remember that same night. However, if it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not apply extra cream to make up for a missed dose. It is okay to occasionally miss a dose — just try to stay on your regular schedule as much as possible.
storage: Store imiquimod cream at room temperature between 36°F and 77°F (2°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat and direct sunlight. Do not freeze this medication. Keep it in its original packaging and out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the cream after the expiration date printed on the package. Each single-use packet should be thrown away after one use — do not save opened packets for later.
what_to_avoid: Avoid sexual contact (vaginal, anal, or oral) while the cream is on your skin. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and tanning beds during treatment, as the treated skin will be more sensitive to sunlight — use sunscreen and protective clothing when outdoors. Do not use other creams, lotions, or medications on the treated area unless your doctor approves. Avoid getting this cream in your eyes, mouth, lips, or inside the vagina or anus. Do not use more cream than prescribed — using too much can cause serious skin reactions. Avoid circumcision or other surgical procedures on the treated area during treatment.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor if you experience severe skin reactions such as intense redness, blistering, open sores, or peeling at the treatment site. Call your doctor if you develop flu-like symptoms such as fever, chills, body aches, or extreme tiredness that interfere with your daily activities. Also call your doctor if you notice signs of a skin infection such as increased warmth, swelling, oozing, or pus. Let your doctor know if your skin does not seem to be improving after several weeks of treatment, or if your condition gets significantly worse. Women should call their doctor if they experience vaginal swelling or discharge.
when_it_works: Imiquimod works slowly over time — do not expect overnight results. For genital warts, you may start to see improvement after a few weeks, but the full treatment course can take up to 16 weeks. For actinic keratosis, the full treatment is 16 weeks. For basal cell carcinoma, the treatment lasts 6 weeks. Some patients notice that the treated area looks worse before it gets better — this is normal and means the medicine is working. After finishing treatment, your doctor will check the area to make sure it has cleared up completely.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Imiquimod is not recommended during pregnancy. Talk to your doctor about safer options if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: It is not known if imiquimod passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before using this medication while breastfeeding, and avoid applying it near the breast or nipple area. Children: Imiquimod is generally not recommended for children under the age of 12. It may be used in children 12 and older for certain conditions under a doctor's supervision. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects and should be monitored closely. Immune system problems: If you have a weakened immune system due to HIV, organ transplant, or medications that suppress immunity, tell your doctor — imiquimod may be less effective and your skin reactions may be more severe.
